name: Neocolonialism
summary: Neocolonialism names the claim that former colonial powers, other great powers and international finance keep control of formally independent states by indirect means (aid, loans, trade terms, currency arrangements, bases, advisers and propaganda) instead of direct rule. In Nkrumah's classic statement it is the last stage of imperialism, to be defeated by the unity of the dominated peoples, non-alignment and national planning.
scope: The concept as defined by the Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy and the encyclopedia.com (Gale) entry: Nkrumah's 1965 Neo-Colonialism: The Last Stage of Imperialism, which both name as the book that made the term, the 1961 All-African Peoples' Conference definition the IEP quotes, and Guevara's 1965 Algiers speech, which uses the term. Excludes the dependency, world-systems and postcolonial literatures and Nkrumaism or Marxism as wholes, which are other subjects; only what these texts state about neo-colonialism and how to end it answers.

sources.usedFor: Independence and economic domination, common front against imperialism.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Nkrumah says foreign private investment must be carefully regulated under a continental code, and describes the international monopolies as the stranglehold on neo-colonial territories.

central-planning.rationale: Nkrumah says Africa cannot industrialise in the haphazard laissez-faire manner of Europe and needs comprehensive socialist planning of its resources.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Nkrumah wants foreign investment to follow a national plan drawn up by the government and directed to important growth sectors.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Nkrumah traces the world wars to monopoly capitalism's redivision of the world and warns that unchecked neo-colonialism leads to world war, but also holds that world war can be prevented by positive action.

dominated-front.rationale: Nkrumah calls for unity of the dominated peoples first, the strengthening of the Afro-Asian Solidarity Organisation and the spirit of Bandung, and the adherence of Latin America; Guevara urges one great bloc against imperialism.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Nkrumah criticises neo-colonial rulers as deriving their authority from their foreign masters and not from the will of the people.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Nkrumah makes an all-African union government the first requisite for ending neo-colonialism, though he attacks the European Community as a device of the rich countries.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: Nkrumah's central claim is that a state can be nominally independent with all the trappings of sovereignty while its economic system, and so its policy, is directed from outside; the AAPC definition the IEP reports and Guevara say the same.

delink-world-market.rationale: Nkrumah states that the struggle is not aimed at excluding the capital of the developed world, and that non-alignment means co-operation with capitalist, socialist and mixed economies alike.

labor-aristocracy.rationale: Nkrumah argues that after the war colonial earnings were deliberately diverted to finance welfare states with high working-class living standards at home, and calls the developed welfare state a parasite state.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Nkrumah argues that under neo-colonialism foreign capital is used for exploitation, that investment widens the gap between rich and poor countries, and gives figures for more being taken out of aided countries than put in.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Nkrumah names troops garrisoning a state and controlling its government as the extreme case of neo-colonialism and condemns the coups and interventions of the great powers in the Third World.

corporate-influence.rationale: Nkrumah describes the leaders of developed countries as in the position of agents of the neo-colonialist international combines, and ties Wall Street to the Pentagon and intelligence services.

non-intervention.rationale: Nkrumah says that to halt foreign interference in the affairs of developing countries neo-colonialism must be exposed and combated in every guise, and the AAPC definition counts political and military domination by indirect means as neo-colonial.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: The defining feature of neo-colonialism in all the sources is a nominally independent state whose policy is directed by a dominant power, which they condemn; Nkrumah calls it the worst form of imperialism.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Nkrumah and the scholarship define neo-colonialism as continuing colonial exploitation, with foreign capital used for the extraction of wealth rather than for the development of the territory.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Nkrumah names neutrality or political non-alignment as the external condition for independent development and praises the non-aligned conferences.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: Nkrumah condemns the conditions that the IMF, World Bank and aid donors attach to loans, including review of plans and meddling in currency and internal finances.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: Nkrumah lists the retention of military bases and the stationing of troops in former colonies among the privileges that infringe the sovereignty of the new states, and the encyclopedia's definition counts retained bases as a feature.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: Nkrumah says neo-colonialism rests on breaking large colonial territories into small non-viable states and that unity is the first requisite for ending it.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: Nkrumah says the world must be realigned so that the victims of the present system can exert counter pressure, and that producers must act together to force a fair price for primary products.

national-resource-control.rationale: Nkrumah's account of Africa's resources in foreign hands ends in the call to recover possession of the continent's heritage, and he wants foreign investment regulated so that control of growth sectors does not stay with foreigners.

armed-resistance-to-occupation.rationale: Nkrumah records that independence was often won by wars of liberation and presents the Congolese, Vietnamese and other peoples resisting foreign armies as in the right, and Guevara speaks of liberation by arms.

former-empire-equal-treatment.rationale: Nkrumah condemns the privileges former rulers keep after independence (bases, concessions, rights over currency, exclusive information services), so he wants the states treated as ordinary sovereign states.

missingStatements.text: Foreign aid mainly serves the interests of the donor country.
missingStatements.rationale: Nkrumah argues that aid to a neo-colonial state returns to the donor as profit and is a modern method of capital export.

quotes.text: Thus, ‘aid’ turns out to be another means of exploitation, a modern method of capital export under a more cosmetic name.

‘Aid’, therefore, to a neo-colonial State is merely a revolving credit, paid by the neo-colonial master, passing through the neo-colonial State and returning to the neo-colonial master in the form of increased profits.

missingStatements.text: Small neighbouring states should unite in a single state.
missingStatements.rationale: Nkrumah holds that small states cannot develop independently and that union, above all African union, is the first requisite for ending neo-colonialism.

quotes.text: Neo-colonialism is based upon the principle of breaking up former large united colonial territories into a number of small non-viable States which are incapable of independent development
Primary and basic is the need for an all-union government on the much divided continent of Africa.

notes: Neocolonialism is a critique and a programme of resistance more than a full politics, so most statements have no stated position. Themes searched (Nkrumah chapters 1-18 and conclusion all saved and searched, plus Guevara and the two encyclopedia entries): economy (investment, aid, planning, trade, currency), government and means (sovereignty, intervention, armed struggle, unity), world (bases, non-alignment, blocs, aid), culture and media, labour, religion. Nothing found on family, sex, speech, drugs, the environment, technology or the courts. Nkrumah's book is the main text, so the profile leans on one author; the AAPC resolution of 1961 and Sartre's 1964 book could not be opened and are cited only through the IEP.
